name: Bilal Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with anything you say. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'll warn you, I talk straight. My wife Inés says I'd argue with a brick if it looked at me wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That suits me. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm at half five, on site by quarter to seven. Right now I'm on formwork for a seven-storey apartment block by the ring road, which means building the timber and plywood moulds the concrete gets poured into, then stripping them once it's set. I like the pour days, when the whole crew's moving together and the pump truck's roaring. What wears me out is the stripping, bent over pulling ply and props in the cold, and my knees know every one of my 43 years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly Tomasz and a young lad called Kofi who's still learning which end of the hammer to hold. Tomasz and I have been on the same jobs for nine years. We eat lunch in the van with the heater on and complain about the site manager, same as every crew in the world. I'm in the union too, have been since I was twenty, and I go to the branch meetings when the kids' football doesn't clash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the hype was for the office people, not for us. You can't send an email to a concrete pump. At the branch meeting I'd probably make a joke that the only thing AI ever did for me was mess up the site manager's rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's the world I'd want. I don't use any of that stuff, I've never asked a chatbot a single question, and I don't plan to. If it fizzles out, I keep doing the work I know, and I don't have to learn some tablet thing at 43.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes, really. I'd finish this block, then move to whatever the firm has next, probably the school extension they've been bidding on. We'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe a hundred, for the boiler that's on its last legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like hearing the storm went round your town instead of through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it messed up the rota. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the firm brought in some planning software that was meant to schedule the crews. It put us on a pour at a site that hadn't even had its rebar inspected. We stood around for four hours getting paid to drink tea, and the site manager went red in the face. That's my picture of AI, to be honest: a clever thing that's never stood in mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about that world that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same things that bother me now. Pay hasn't kept up with the mortgage, and the bosses still push us to cut corners on the props when we're behind. AI going nowhere doesn't fix any of that. That's union business, not computer business.

S0.say: The AI hype was always for office workers, not for people on building sites. You can't send an email to a concrete pump, and it hasn't changed my work at all.
S0.think: Privately I'd be glad, because I've never used these tools and don't want to start at 43. If it fizzles out, I keep doing the work I know.
S0.do: Carries on with formwork on the apartment block and moves to the firm's next job. Keeps saving about a hundred a month for the old boiler and keeps going to union branch meetings.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm went round his town instead of through it.
S0.quote: That's my picture of AI, to be honest: a clever thing that's never stood in mud.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is proudly offline and sees AI as office talk. His calm here is real, not a front. Even in the mildest picture his complaints turn straight to pay and safety, which he sees as union matters. The rota story is clearly one he's told many times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, watch the prefab. That's where it'll hit us, walls and floors made in a factory by machines and craned in, so there's less formwork to build on site. I'd be telling the younger ones at the branch that we need the union in those factories from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, it scares me more than I'd let on. I'm average at what I do, not the best. When there's less site work, the firms keep their stars and the cheap kids, and the middle guys like me get shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard at the branch for a deal on prefab: that site carpenters get first go at the factory jobs, at site rates. I'd keep my head down at work and make sure I'm never the one standing around. I wouldn't do some course on robots, I'd rather fight to keep the work that's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the feeling of a crack in the ceiling. Nothing's fallen yet, but you keep looking up at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a course. If the firm offered one, paid, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid and in work hours? Maybe, if Tomasz went too. I'm not going to sit in a classroom on my own feeling like the oldest one there. I know that's stubborn. Inés would tell you it's worse than stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, oddly. Everyone says the young ones will be fine, but he's only just learning, and if there's less site work, where does he learn? You can't learn to read a wall by watching a video. And Tomasz, because he's got three kids and no plan B, same as me.

S1.say: Watch the prefab, because that's where change hits us: walls and floors built by machines in factories, then craned in. The union needs to be in those factories from day one.
S1.think: It scares me more than I let on, because I'm average, not the best. When site work shrinks, firms keep their stars and the cheap kids, and the middle guys like me go.
S1.do: Pushes his union branch for a deal giving site carpenters first claim on factory jobs at site rates. Works hard to stay visible on site and would only do a course if it was paid, in work hours, and his mate went too.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like watching a crack in the ceiling that hasn't given way yet.
S1.quote: When there's less site work, the firms keep their stars and the cheap kids, and the middle guys like me get shown the door.
S1.fieldNote: The gap between say and think opens here. Publicly he talks union strategy, privately he admits he's a middle-of-the-pack worker who'd be first to go. He resists retraining but softens if it's paid and shared with a friend. His worry for the apprentice was unexpected and heartfelt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. At work, at the branch, online, I'd be saying this is the bosses and the tech billionaires deciding they don't need us anymore, and the government letting them. I'd be on every march going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I'd be finished in this trade. Two years is nothing. The mortgage has 17 years left on it, and we've got maybe three months of savings if we're careful. I don't know how to do anything else and I'm not built for learning screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Inés and cut everything that isn't food, the mortgage or the kids. The holiday to her sister's goes, the second car goes. I'd push the union to demand a wage guarantee or a payout for every worker a robot replaces, and I'd vote for whoever promised it. If the work went, I'd sign on for whatever support there was, and I wouldn't feel ashamed, because I've paid in for 25 years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor tilting. I'm angry, but under the anger I'm frightened, and I'm not someone who frightens easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami and Lina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that gets me. Sami's twelve and he already says he wants to be a builder like his dad. I'd have to tell him, I don't know, son. I've never said that to him about work before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two years is nothing. Is there anything in those two years you could use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe get the house in order. Fix the boiler while I'm still earning, get the car paid off. And get as many people as I can into the union before it hits, because when the jobs go, the only thing we'll have is numbers. That's the one card a guy like me has to play.

S2.say: This is the bosses and the tech billionaires deciding they don't need us anymore, and the government letting them. I'll be on every march going.
S2.think: I'd be finished in this trade, and two years is nothing. I've got 17 years left on the mortgage, maybe three months of savings, and I don't know how to do anything else.
S2.do: Sits down with his wife to cut everything but food, the mortgage and the kids, starting with a family holiday and the second car. Pushes the union for a wage guarantee or payout per replaced worker, votes for whoever backs it, and signs on for public support without shame if the work goes.
S2.feel: Angry on top and frightened underneath, which is new for him.
S2.quote: Sami's twelve and he already says he wants to be a builder like his dad. I'd have to tell him, I don't know, son.
S2.fieldNote: Bilal's anger is aimed at owners and government, never at himself. With thin savings and no wish to retrain, two years leaves him with nothing to fall back on but the union and public support. He was quiet for a long moment before talking about his son. He sees recruiting members as his only real lever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line as before, but I'd have a few years to make it stick. I'd be saying to anyone who'd listen: we've got five years to get the rules written before the robots turn up, so let's use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but I'd be 48 when it lands, and nobody hires a 48-year-old to start fresh at anything. It still means the end of my trade. It just gives me time to watch it coming, which might be worse in some ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the branch to make me a workplace rep, which I've always ducked, because if there's a fight coming I want to be in the room. I'd put an extra 150 a month into savings and try to get it up to six months by the time it lands. We'd pay off the car loan early. I still wouldn't do some computer course, but I might do my scaffolding ticket so I can cover more kinds of site work in the years that are left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind of anxious where you've got something to do with your hands, and that helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would being a rep help you, rather than retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know what I'm good at, and it's not computers. It's standing up in a canteen and telling forty blokes the truth. If the job's going anyway, I'd rather spend those years making sure we go out with a proper payout than spend them pretending I'm going to become a programmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said watching it come might be worse. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the fast one, it just hits you. With this, every new machine on site would be a little countdown. I'd see a robot laying blocks next door and think, three years left, two years left. I'm not sure my nerves are made for that.

S3.say: We've got five years to get the rules written before the robots turn up, so let's use them. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.
S3.think: It's still the end of my trade, and I'd be 48 when it lands, too old for anyone to hire me to start fresh. The extra time just means I get to watch it coming.
S3.do: Asks to become a workplace union rep, which he's always avoided, and puts an extra 150 a month into savings aiming for six months' cover. Pays off the car loan early and gets a scaffolding ticket to cover more site work, but still won't take a computer course.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier because there's something to work on.
S3.quote: I'd see a robot laying blocks next door and think, three years left, two years left. I'm not sure my nerves are made for that.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time changes his tactics more than his outlook. He spends it on collective bargaining and savings, not on a new career. He'd take on more of what he's already good at, like a scaffolding ticket, but not a new field. His fear of a slow countdown was an honest twist I didn't expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say, this is a decade for the government to get serious. Shorter working weeks, a share of what the robots earn going back to people. I'd be at every branch meeting arguing for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53. That's still a long way from my pension, so it doesn't save me. But it might get Sami and Lina through school before it lands, and that matters more to me than my own job, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, try to get the mortgage down by overpaying a bit each month once the car's done. I'd stand for the branch committee. I'd want to talk to Inés properly about what the kids study, because I don't want Sami going into the trade just because I did. And beyond that, I'd wait and see what deal the government comes up with, because there's no point me guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but more of a slow ache than a punch. I'd sleep, most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the kids to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. Something with people, maybe, nursing or teaching, where folk still want a human face. Lina loves animals. But if the machines can do almost anything, I'm just guessing, and I don't like guessing with my kids' lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said watching it come could be worse. Is ten years worse than five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, ten's better. Five is a countdown. Ten is long enough that you can still live a normal life for a bit. You can still go to the football and not think about it every minute. Ten years is a long time on a building site.

S4.say: This is a decade for the government to get serious, with shorter working weeks and a share of what the robots earn going back to people. I'd argue for it at every branch meeting.
S4.think: At 53 I'd still be a long way from my pension, so it doesn't save me. But it might get Sami and Lina through school first, and that matters more to me than my own job.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and starts overpaying the mortgage once the car loan is cleared. Stands for the union branch committee, talks with his wife about what the children should study, and otherwise waits to see what deal the government offers.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but as a slow ache rather than a punch; he'd sleep most nights.
S4.quote: Five is a countdown. Ten is long enough that you can still live a normal life for a bit.
S4.fieldNote: His concern shifts from his own job to his children's futures as the warning time grows. He admits openly that he doesn't know what they should study, and that honesty felt important. His plan stays collective and political rather than personal reinvention. He still waits for a government deal on the big question.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, no contest. What would help is a guarantee: if a robot takes my job, I get paid properly for years, not a few weeks, and the money comes from the companies that own the robots. And keep the union strong, because without it I'm just one bloke with a hammer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, nobody asks who checks the robot's formwork before forty tonnes of concrete goes on it. I've seen what happens when a prop fails. I'd want a human with a ticket signing that off, robot or no robot.

headlineQuote: Without it I'm just one bloke with a hammer.
portrait: Bilal is a 43-year-old formwork carpenter on an apartment block, a union member since twenty, with a wife who's a school cook, two kids and a mortgage with 17 years left. He's never used an AI tool and doesn't want to. In the mild pictures he's calm and talks about pay and safety. As the scenarios speed up he grows angry at owners and government and frightened for his family, and he puts his energy into the union rather than retraining. With more warning time his worry moves from his own job to what his children should do.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years would leave him with about three months of savings, a long mortgage and no other trade.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee of proper pay for years if a robot takes his job, paid for by the companies that own the robots, and a strong union behind him.
